description: Ember Almanac harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire hot-spot records into one continuous global record, bridging differences in resolution, overpass time and detection threshold. It offers an interactive map, a daily "right now" view and a model of where and when fires are likely. Built on FIRMS data, Cloud Build and GitHub Pages. Seeking teammates in remote sensing, data viz, frontend or science communication.
summary: Satellites have recorded active fires every day since 2000, but the record is split: MODIS sees 1 km pixels, VIIRS (from 2012) sees 375 m pixels and reports about four times more detections from the same fires. Spliced together, the raw records make every place on Earth appear to quadruple its burning in 2012. And on 2 November 2026 the record broke again, when Suomi NPP, the satellite behind the VIIRS record, delivered its last fire data. Ember Almanac harmonizes 491 million NASA FIRMS detections from four satellites into one consistent record, from November 2000 to this week, and turns it into a burning activity calendar for any area a user draws. It learns a local, seasonal exchange rate between MODIS and VIIRS from the years both flew, restates the MODIS era in VIIRS terms with an uncertainty interval, and carries the record on with NOAA-20 now that Suomi NPP has stopped. For a selected area the web app shows when burning normally starts, peaks and ends, a day-by-day calendar of every year since 2000, the periods that broke the pattern, the long-term trend, and how the last two weeks compare with normal. It gives responders, land managers and scientists a like-for-like view of 26 years of fire, in the browser, with no account or download.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ember Almanac is a web application. The map shows where the planet typically burns in each month, which month each place burns most, or the local exchange rate between the sensors. The user draws a box (or opens a preset such as Northern Thailand, Punjab, the Amazon's arc of deforestation or Boreal Canada) and gets an "almanac" for that area:

• The fire season: the shortest window that holds 80% of a normal year's burning and the normal peak date, or each burning period where a place has several (for example the two harvest pulses of Punjab).

• A burning calendar with one row per year and one mark per day, from 2000 to the current week.

• A "right now" line: the last two weeks against the same two weeks in every earlier year.

• Any year laid over the normal seasonal cycle (median, middle half and 10–90th percentile of all years).

• Yearly totals with an 80% interval on estimated years, a Theil–Sen trend and a Mann–Kendall significance test.

• A ranked list of unusual episodes: runs of five or more days above the 90th percentile for that time of year.

• A CSV export of the daily record and a shareable link.

HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS

(1) All sensors are screened by the same rules (vegetation fires only, low-confidence detections removed) and counted on one 0.25° daily grid, keeping Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 separate.

(2) For every grid cell and calendar month we estimate the ratio of VIIRS to MODIS detections from the overlap years. The ratio is not a constant: it runs from 2.6× to 6.3× across the burning world.

(3) A hierarchy (global → 5° block → 1° cell → 0.25° cell) shrinks each ratio toward its parent with a gamma-Poisson prior, so busy cells keep their own ratio and sparse cells borrow from their neighbourhood.

(4) Ratios are learned only from 2012–2021, before Terra and Aqua began drifting from their nominal orbits.

(5) Before 2012 the record is MODIS × ratio (a separate ratio for the Terra-only months of 2000–02). From 2012 to 2 November 2026 it is Suomi NPP VIIRS as observed.

(6) After Suomi NPP stopped, and on 68 earlier days when it was down (found automatically: the global VIIRS/MODIS ratio sits near 4 every day, and below 2 means the sensor was not observing), the record continues on NOAA-20 VIIRS. We tested a local ratio for that hand-over against a single factor on held-out years; the local ratio did not help, so the simpler factor (1.018×) is used.

(7) The current year comes from the FIRMS API. Near-real-time detections have no fire-type label yet, so each cell's count is scaled by the share of vegetation fires that cell showed in 2023–2025, which removes gas flares, industry and volcanoes.

(8) The browser receives the raw counts of all four satellites plus the ratios and applies the harmonization itself, so every number can be inspected.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

We backcast: ratios learned from 2015–2021, then MODIS alone used to rebuild 2012–2014 and compared with what VIIRS recorded. Splicing raw counts is biased by −75%. A single global factor has a typical error of 35% per 1° cell and month. Ember Almanac brings that to 26% with +0.4% bias, and to 10% at the scale of a region and a year, where 74% of estimates fall within ±25% of the truth (50% for the global factor). The hand-over to NOAA-20 is tested forward in time (fitted on 2018–2022, checked on 2023–2025): 13% typical error per 1° cell and month, 4% per region and year, +0.2% bias.

BENEFITS

Fire managers can compare a current season with seasons before 2012 on the same scale, and keep doing so now that Suomi NPP has retired. Early-warning teams get the normal start, peak and end of burning for any district. Researchers get a documented, reproducible, validated harmonized series for any box on Earth.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Python, DuckDB and NumPy for the pipeline, run on Google Cloud Build; static binary tiles on Google Cloud Storage; a static web app in TypeScript, React, Vite and MapLibre GL on GitHub Pages; Remotion for the demo video. There is no backend: the browser loads only the tiles an area touches and computes the statistics locally. Source code: https://github.com/weifish0/ember-almanac

LIMITS WE STATE IN THE APP

A detection is a hot pixel at overpass time, not a fire or a burned area. Cloud and smoke hide fires. Harmonization restores how much burned, not the exact day, so the pre-2012 record should be read at weekly scale or coarser. The newest weeks are near-real-time data. The published record runs to 14 November 2026; rerunning the pipeline extends it.

USE OF AI

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used to write the pipeline, the web application and the video composition, and to help analyse results, under the team's direction and review. The voice-over in the demo video was generated with Google Gemini TTS from the team's own script, using a team member's own voice. No AI-generated images or video are used: every map, chart and number is computed from the NASA data listed below. NASA branding is not used.

REFERENCES

Giglio, L., Schroeder, W., Justice, C. O. (2016). The collection 6 MODIS active fire detection algorithm and fire products. Remote Sensing of Environment, 178, 31–41.

Schroeder, W., Oliva, P., Giglio, L., Csiszar, I. A. (2014). The New VIIRS 375 m active fire detection data product. Remote Sensing of Environment, 143, 85–96.

Open-source software: DuckDB, NumPy, pandas, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Remotion; Fraunces and Instrument Sans typefaces (SIL Open Font License).
